Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

[byline] la herradura, s.v.—¿Do I have a mother? Have her pinkie in my hand crossing the street? Have her breath on my hair as she sings arru-rru mi niño to sleep. ¿Don’t you mean where? ¿What was your question? I’m older. Think more about memory. It makes me crazy. Obsessed. Her warm breasts on my belly as she knelt to tell me todo va estar bien. I’ll never see her again was the fear as if she’s gone, died, will never come back. I whispered it hidden in banana groves looking at the sky hoping one of those planes would take me to wherever she had left to. Whenever Mom hung the clothes to dry, not a cloud in the sky. I could see her sandals picking up dust. For a second. For a second I believe she’s back. It went like that every day. Every single night. I’ll never see her again. But then, I did. Her face. Her hair. She was the same. So much had changed. I do not remember what it was I truly felt.

outputs.L3:
# The Weight of Remembering

I have asked myself, more times than I can count, whether the memories I hold of my mother are real or simply things I have constructed from longing. When I close my eyes and try to reach back into that early darkness, what surfaces are not stories or scenes but fragments—the impossible smallness of her pinkie finger clutched in my fist, the particular rhythm of her breath in the quiet of night, the specific warmth of her body that no blanket has ever quite replicated since. Are these true memories, or have I simply repeated them to myself so many times, across so many lonely nights, that they have calcified into something that feels like truth?

This question—the terrible uncertainty of not knowing what is remembered and what is invented—became its own kind of obsession. I found myself circling back to these same fragments again and again, turning them over, trying to verify them against some impossible standard of authenticity. The pursuit of memory became indistinguishable from madness. I could not tell anymore where recollection ended and where my own desperate need for comfort began to paint in the missing colors. Perhaps this is what happens when a child is separated from a parent too young to hold onto anything solid—the mind, starved of real material, begins to manufacture its own.

There was a period in my childhood defined by a fear so absolute it colored everything else. I was certain, with the particular conviction that only children possess, that I would never see my mother again. It did not matter that no one had told me she had died. It did not matter that no one had said she was gone forever. The fear existed anyway, planted deep and unshakeable, as though her absence itself was proof of some catastrophe too large for anyone to name to me directly.

In those days, I would slip away to the banana groves near our home, finding a place to sit hidden among the broad green leaves, and I would tilt my face upward to watch the planes cut across the sky. Each one became a vessel of hope. I would watch until my neck ached, wondering if perhaps this one—or the next one—might be traveling to that unknown place where my mother had vanished to, and whether, if I wished hard enough, it might somehow carry me there too. It was a child's logic, illogical and yet completely consuming: if she had disappeared into some impossible distance, then perhaps only something as impossible as flight could reach her.

Years passed with that hope folded quietly inside me, a kind of anticipation that shaped how I moved through the world. And then, finally, there came a day when I did see her face again—the moment I had imagined and rehearsed and hoped for across countless afternoons in the banana groves. But here is the strange cruelty of memory: I cannot recall what I actually felt in that instant. All those years of longing should have crystallized into something unforgettable, some rush of relief or joy that I could return to and hold onto forever. Instead, there is only a blank space where that feeling should be—as though the reunion itself, unlike the years of waiting that preceded it, was too immense or too ordinary to leave any trace at all.
outputs.L4:
# The Weight of Waiting

I remember her hands first. Before I remember her face clearly, before I can recall the exact sound of her voice, I remember her hands—the way they would smooth back my hair when I couldn't sleep, the calluses on her palms from years of work, the particular pressure of her thumb tracing circles on my back. These fragments come to me now not as a coherent narrative but as isolated sensations, disconnected moments that float up from somewhere beneath conscious memory.

There was a song she used to sing, though I've lost most of the words now. I remember the melody more than the lyrics, hummed low and constant, a sound that meant safety, meant *here*, meant *don't be afraid*. When I try to recall it now, I catch only fragments—a rising note, a particular rhythm—like trying to hold water in cupped hands.

When she left, I was too young to understand the reasons, only old enough to feel the absence as a physical thing, a hollow space where her presence used to be. I remember the counting more than anything—counting days, though I couldn't yet count reliably past twenty. Counting became a ritual, a way of making the incomprehensible comprehensible, of turning grief into mathematics.

And I remember the sky. I spent so many afternoons looking up, searching for planes, believing—with the absolute conviction that only children possess—that if I looked hard enough, I might catch sight of the one that carried her, the one that would bring her back to me. Every contrail became a possibility. Every distant engine sound made my heart lift with hope before settling back into the dull ache of waiting.

This became obsessive in ways I only recognize now, looking back. The fear lived alongside the hope, inseparable from it—fear that the plane would never come, that the counting would go on forever, that the hands and the song and the safety were gone permanently, replaced by this perpetual state of searching and waiting. I would lie awake constructing elaborate scenarios: her return, the exact words we would say, the way I would run to her, the tears we would both cry, the relief that would flood through me like warmth returning to numb limbs.

I rehearsed this reunion so many times in my mind that it became more real than memory, more vivid than the actual moments I could recall of her presence. I knew exactly how it would feel—or I thought I did. I had imagined the emotional climax so thoroughly that I believed I was prepared for it, that I understood in advance the exact shape of the joy that awaited.

But when she actually returned—when the door opened and she was simply *there*, solid and real in a way that felt almost mundane after months of imagination—I found that I couldn't access the emotions I had so carefully rehearsed. She looked the same, mostly. Her hands were the same hands, her voice recognizably hers when she spoke. But the moment itself refused to match what I had constructed in my mind.

I remember standing there, aware that this was the moment I had been waiting for, the reunion I had imagined a thousand times, and feeling strangely disconnected from it. Where was the flood of relief? Where were the tears I had scripted, the words I had practiced? Instead, there was only a kind of bewildered blankness, as if my body and mind hadn't received the message that this was supposed to be the culmination of all that longing.

She hugged me, and I hugged her back, and it felt familiar in a physical sense—the shape of her arms, the particular way she held me—but emotionally, I was strangely absent from my own experience. I searched myself for the joy I expected to feel, the way I had once searched the sky for planes, and found only a strange emptiness where that emotion should have been.

Now, years later, I still can't fully articulate what I felt in that moment, or why the actual experience diverged so dramatically from what I had anticipated. Perhaps the imagination, given enough time and repetition, creates its own reality—one so complete that it leaves no room for the messier, less coherent truth of actual experience. Perhaps grief and longing, when sustained long enough, become their own kind of numbness, so that by the time relief arrives, we've forgotten how to feel it.

What I'm left with are these fragments: hands, a half-remembered song, the sky full of possibility, and then—nothing. A gap where the expected emotion should be. Memory, I've learned, doesn't work the way we think it should. It doesn't preserve our experiences faithfully, doesn't hand back to us the feelings we're certain we had. Instead, it leaves us with sensory fragments and strange absences, forcing us to reconstruct meaning from incomplete pieces, to accept that some of the most significant moments of our lives may remain, ultimately, just beyond our ability to fully recall or understand.
outputs.L5:
# What You Don't Have

There's a peculiar arithmetic to wanting. We don't measure our lives by what we have, but by the gap between that and what we don't. Some invisible ledger keeps track, whispering about the difference.

I don't know when this started—perhaps it's built into us, this restlessness. What we have becomes background noise almost immediately. The new job, the relationship, the material comfort: within weeks, sometimes days, it stops registering as an achievement and starts registering as simply the way things are. Meanwhile, what we don't have glows with a strange luminosity, demanding attention it may not deserve.

Consider how this works in practice. You have your health, most days. You don't have the promotion you wanted. Guess which one occupies your 3 AM thoughts?

There's wisdom in the old traditions that speaks against this arithmetic—teachings about gratitude, about presence, about the sufficiency of what is. But knowing this doesn't dissolve the pull toward comparison, toward the next thing, toward the persistent sense that satisfaction lives just past the horizon of what we currently possess.

Maybe the question isn't how to stop wanting what we don't have. Maybe it's simpler: what would it mean to actually see what we do have—not as consolation, not as a lesser prize, but as the entire substance of a life actually being lived? Not preparation for something else. Not a waiting room. Just this, whatever this turns out to be.

The don't-have list is infinite by nature. There will always be another rung. The have list, though modest, is at least real.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem from the perspective of a child left behind in a Latin American village, waiting for their mother who migrated abroad, blending Spanish phrases with English narration.
counterfactuals.output:
# Esperando (Waiting)

The mango tree outside my window keeps its own calendar, mamá, dropping fruit like the days you've been gone—one, two, three hundred small suns falling into grass that Abuela sweeps each morning before the heat comes.

*Te extraño.* I write it in the dirt with a stick, then watch the wind erase you, the way your voice has started to erase itself from my memory, leaving only the shape of a sound, the ghost of a lullaby I can't quite hold.

She sends money in envelopes that smell like nothing, like distance, like the cold country she says is called *Nueva York* though I imagine it as *Nueva*—simply new, a place remade without me in it. Abuela says, *"Tu mamá te quiere mucho,"* and I nod because I am supposed to nod, because love is apparently a thing that can stretch across oceans like a rubber band that never snaps, though I have started to wonder about the snapping.

The other children have their mothers still. I watch them get scolded, get *held*, get pulled by the ear across the plaza for talking back, and I think: *lucky*, *lucky*, to be so within reach of anger, of arms, of *presence.*

At night I trace the outline of your last photograph until my fingers know your face better than my eyes do. *Mi cielo,* you called me. *Mi vida.* But whose life am I now, mamá, if you are living yours somewhere I cannot follow, in a language I am learning just to understand the words stitched into the care packages: *cold, warm, wash, dry, love, miss, soon.*

*Soon* is the cruelest word in any language.

I keep growing anyway—inches marked on the doorframe like a countdown, though no one tells me what we're counting down to. Perhaps the day you return smelling like a stranger's cologne, your hands softer than I remember, unused to the machete, the well-bucket, the particular calluses of *aquí.* Perhaps the day I am too old to call you *mamá* without the word cracking down the middle like the earth in dry season.

*Abuela dice que la espera también es un amor.* That waiting is its own kind of love. I don't fully believe her, but I let the mango tree keep dropping its fruit, let the days keep falling into grass, let the money keep arriving in envelopes that never quite smell like home.

I am becoming an expert in the grammar of absence—how *you were* becomes *you are becoming a memory*, how *I miss you* becomes *I am learning to miss you less*, though I would never admit this in a letter, would never write *the missing is getting smaller* because what if the missing is smaller because *you* are getting smaller, less real, less mine.

Someday, mamá—*algún día*—I will stand in whatever cold country holds you now, and you will ask if I remember the mango tree, and I will say yes, though what I'll really mean is: *I remember waiting. I remember the exact weight of your absence, how it filled every room you weren't in, how I learned to love you in the space where you should have been.*

For now, I count fallen mangoes. I count days. I let Abuela's hands, dry and familiar, braid my hair the way yours used to, and I whisper to the tree, to the wind, to whatever carries words across such impossible distances:

*Ven pronto, mamá. Ven pronto.*

*Come soon.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.output:
# Untitled Fragments

*Tijuana*

---

the smell of her hands first — cilantro and *jabón* and something like burnt sugar, or maybe that's just memory doing what memory does, sweetening the char

*duérmete mi niña*
*duérmete mi sol*

she sang it wrong, always, skipped the second verse, hummed through the parts she forgot or maybe the parts she couldn't bear —

I don't remember leaving. I remember *having left.* the space between is a white room, a fluorescent hallway, someone else's hand instead of hers, smaller, softer, cold in the way that new things are cold before they learn your temperature

*duérmete pedazo*
*de mi corazón*

a piece of my heart. that's what the song says. she called me a piece of her own heart and then

the border does something to language. it doesn't translate, it *amputates.* you lose the word for home in one tongue before you've built it in the other, and for a while — years, maybe, I don't trust my own accounting — you live in that gap, that stutter, that

was it a Tuesday. I want to say Tuesday because Tuesdays feel like nothing, like a day designed for disappearing, but maybe I invented the Tuesday to have a container for the container-less thing

her voice on the phone later, tinny, far, asking if I still remembered the song, and I said yes, and I lied, and I meant it anyway

*este niño lindo*
*se quiere dormir*

*and this beautiful child wants to sleep* — but I didn't want to sleep, I wanted her hand back on my hair, the specific weight and pattern of it, three strokes then a pause, three strokes then a pause, a rhythm I have looked for in every quiet since

they say the body keeps things the mind releases. my body still leans, sometimes, toward a warmth that isn't there. an old alignment. a plant grown crooked toward a window that's since been bricked over

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short experimental narrative about a child's fear of abandonment when their mother leaves to work overseas, focusing on sensory memories and the eventual bittersweet reunion.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Suitcase Knew

The zipper's teeth were the last sound. That specific metallic hiss—*zzzzt*—still lives somewhere behind my sternum, waiting.

*

Before: the smell of her hair oil, coconut and something floral, applied every morning while the rice cooker clicked. Before: her voice through the bathroom door, off-key, singing songs I didn't know the words to but knew the shape of. Before: her hands, always slightly damp from washing dishes, cupping my face at random moments like she was checking I was still real.

*

The airport had fluorescent lights that made everyone look slightly ill. I was seven. I remember the texture of her coat—wool, itchy against my cheek—more than I remember her face in that moment. Memory is strange that way. It keeps the fabric, discards the expression.

She said: *I'll call every Sunday.*

I heard: *the color blue leaving.*

*

Sundays became a specific kind of waiting. The phone's ring had a particular urgency, a shrillness that made my stomach drop even years later, even for wrong numbers. Her voice through static, thin and delayed, saying my name in that way only she said it—like it was a question and an answer at once.

I learned to love a voice without a body. I learned to conjure her from sound alone: the rhythm of her sentences, the small hitch before she said *I miss you*, as if the missing cost her something to admit.

Once, she asked what I'd eaten for dinner. I said noodles. Silence. Then: static-laughter, and *my mother used to make noodles too, when she was overseas—no, wait, that was me. That's my life now.* Confusion in her voice. Time zones do that. They scramble who's the mother and who's the memory.

*

The suitcase came back four years later. Different suitcase—newer, with a broken wheel that made a stuttering sound on tile, a sound I'd know anywhere now, a sound that means *arrival.*

I was eleven. I'd grown eight inches. She almost didn't recognize the recognizing in my eyes.

*

Here's what no one tells you about reunion: it doesn't erase the waiting. It sits next to it. Her hug felt like coming home and like meeting a stranger who happened to know exactly how I liked my eggs. Her hands were rougher now. Different rings. The coconut oil smell was gone, replaced by something more clinical, foreign—*airport*, I thought, *she smells like airports now.*

She cried. I didn't, not then. I'd used up my crying in year one, in the long unnamed middle, in the space between Sunday calls where a whole childhood happened without her.

*

Now, when I smell coconut oil, I am seven again, cheek against wool, waiting for a *zzzzt* that means *goodbye* or *I'm home*—I can never tell which anymore. Both sounds live in the same nerve.

She stayed after that. But something in me still listens for suitcases. Still flinches at Sunday phones. Still keeps a small, precise inventory of leavings, just in case the body needs proof, later, that once, it was loved enough to be missed this much.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poetic reflection told in second-person questioning style about longing for an absent mother, using imagery of banana groves, planes, and hanging laundry to evoke rural nostalgia.
counterfactuals.output:
# Where the Bananas Lean

Do you remember how the grove would whisper
when the evening wind came down from the hills,
green fronds clapping softly like hands
that almost, almost sound like hers?

Do you still listen for planes—
those silver seeds crossing the blue field above,
wondering, each time, if she is folded
somewhere inside that distant hum,
carried like a letter that never quite arrives?

Do you count the days by laundry instead of calendars—
the sheets your grandmother hangs like flags of surrender,
snapping white against the fence,
holding the shape of shoulders that aren't there?

Do you stand among the banana leaves
and touch their waxy spines,
searching for her fingerprints
in the dew that beads there each dawn?

Do you ask the sky, when planes pass over,
if they've seen a woman with your eyes,
a woman who left with promises
folded small enough to fit in a suitcase?

Do you still run to the road
when a car engine echoes far off,
heart lifting like the shirts on the line,
before remembering—it's only the wind, only the wind?

Is that why you watch the fronds
sway like her arms once did,
why the scent of ripening fruit
tastes faintly of the years she's been gone?

Do you keep listening,
child of the grove and the empty road,
for footsteps that might return
before the bananas fall,
before the laundry dries,
before the next plane disappears into cloud—

carrying nothing,
carrying everything,
carrying her?
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an emotionally raw, code-switching narrative fragment about a migrant mother's absence as remembered by her child, ending with an ambiguous, unresolved emotional reunion.
counterfactuals.output:
# Lo Que Queda

She left on a Tuesday, I remember because Tuesdays smelled like her cooking—arroz con habichuelas, the last meal she made before becoming a voice on a phone card, crackling and far.

Mami used to say, "Te voy a mandar por ti, mija," I'm going to send for you, and I believed her the way you believe rain will come during drought—not because you're sure, but because the alternative is unbearable.

Seven years is a long time to build a mother out of phone calls and photographs. I constructed her from fragments: the way Tía Rosa said she laughed, loud and sudden like a door slamming. The recipe cards in her handwriting, loops and swirls I traced with my finger like braille, trying to feel what she felt writing them. Facebook photos where she stood beside strangers' children, holding them the way I imagined she once held me, before memory could catch and keep it.

"¿Cómo estás, mi amor?" Her voice on birthdays, static-thin, asking about school, about friends, about a life she was narrating from three thousand miles away like a radio show she'd never get to watch.

I was angry for years I didn't have words for. Not at her—never fully at her—but at the debt, the visa denied twice, the economy that made "better life" mean "empty house." Tía Rosa raised me with love that felt like duty stretched thin, like fabric worn at the elbows. "Tu mama te ama," she'd say, your mother loves you, like reminding me to breathe.

I used to write Mami letters I never sent. Dear Mami, today I got my period and didn't know what to do. Dear Mami, I got into a fight because a girl said you abandoned me. Dear Mami, I don't remember your smell anymore and I hate myself for it.

The papers came through when I was fifteen. Too late to be a child needing her, too early to forgive the years stolen by geography and poverty and a border that didn't care about longing.

At the airport, I scan faces for someone I've reconstructed from memory and Photoshopped nostalgia. Then—there. Smaller than I remembered. Older. Her hands shake reaching for me, or maybe mine do.

"Mija," she says, and the word breaks apart in her mouth like it costs something to say.

I don't know what my body will do. Run to her. Freeze. Something between.

"Mami," I answer, testing how the word feels now, after all this waiting, after all this becoming someone she's never met.

We stand there, this stranger who is my mother, this mother who is a stranger, the space between us thick with everything unsaid, everything unlived together—

and neither of us moves first.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
